newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Top S.Korea carmakers close ranks against Samsung.
newsitem.headline: Top S.Korea carmakers close ranks against Samsung.

text.p: The move by South Korea's two largest carmakers to inject cash into a core unit of the troubled Kia Group signals a joint effort by existing auto companies to block newcomer Samsung, analysts said on Friday.

Kia announced on Thursday that Hyundai Motor, the country's largest carmaker, and unlisted Daewoo Motor Co had agreed in principle to buy stakes in Kia Steel Co, a specialty steelmaker that is one of Kia's weakest affiliates.
Kia Group's flagship is Kia Motors Corp.

Under the agreement, Hyundai, Daewoo and Kia would form a consortium with each having equal stakes to run Kia Steel. A Kia statement said the three companies had agreed to start working-level negotiations to sort out details.
Analysts said the agreement, which would ease pressures on Kia in negotiations with creditors, underscored concerns about Samsung Group's entry into South Korea's crowded car industry.
"What this highlights is the growing alliance between the three companies. There is a lot of bad blood between Kia and Samsung," said Hun Sok Kang, auto analyst at ING Barings.
Henry Morris, managing director of Coryo International (H.K.) Ltd, said Hyundai and Daewoo made a key defensive move.

"They wanted to keep Kia Motors from falling into the hands of Samsung. This also gets the public used to the idea of them assisting Kia, possibly paving the way for them to make a bid for Kia Motors," Morris said.

While Samsung has consistently denied any interest in acquiring Kia Motors, it was a leaked internal Samsung report suggesting the need for restructuring the country's auto industry that accelerated Kia Group's current crisis.
Samsung has said it would begin producing passenger cars from next March with production reaching 80,000 units in the first year.
Analysts said Samsung was still interested in acquiring Kia Motors as a short-cut into the industry's top ranks, although public opinion may cause it to delay revealing its interest.
"Samsung is not going to give up. Right now Samsung is doing everything it can to facilitate takeover of Kia," said Nam Seung-soo, auto analyst at Daishin Economic Research Institute.
"Given what has been happening, Samsung would want to wait for things to quiet down," said Kang of ING Barings.
The agreement on Kia Steel came on the eve of a crucial meeting of Kia creditors to discuss steps on the fate of the embattled conglomerate. Creditors were set to meet at 0600 GMT.
Kia creditors failed to produce a detailed bailout plan at a meeting on Wednesday after ruling that the group's self-rescue plans were not sufficient.

Creditors put Kia Group under their protection on July 15 after determining that Kia affiliates were on the verge of defaulting on debt payments. Kia's debts totalled 9.5 trillion won ($10.6 billion) as of the end of May.
Creditors have demanded that executives of the eighth-ranked business resign and that Asia Motors, the group's commercial vehicle maker, be sold.

In a desperate move before Wednesday's meetings, Kia announced harsher self-rescue measures, including a cut in the number of its domestic units to five from the current 28 through sell-offs, mergers and spin-offs.

Kia also said Asia Motors would sell off part of its assets before being absorbed by Kia Motors to serve as assembly plants. But creditors said they worried that the plan would worsen the financial status of the flagship.
